newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. Fed seen raising rates next week.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. Fed seen raising rates next week.

text.p: A torrent of expansionary U.S. economic data and hawkish comments by Federal Reserve officials raised the odds of an interest rate hike next week, said economists in a Reuters poll.

Thirty-four of 48 economists at banks, securities firms, consultancies and academic institutions said they expect the Fed to raise the key federal funds rate to at least 5.50 percent at the March 25 monetary policy meeting.
That compares with 17 of 44 who made that projection in a Reuters survey last week.
In addition, 10 experts called for a tightening at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting in May, and four said the Fed is on hold for the foreseeable future.
Among primary dealers, the consensus was even more tightly formed, with 29 of 37 projecting a rate hike as early as next week.

Most of the experts who now predict imminently tighter credit said the move would be the "preemptive strike" Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan again mentioned in his Thursday testimony before Congress's Joint Economic Committee.
Greenspan said the economy retains a "great deal of vigor," and he underscored that an immediate shift in monetary policy would not affect inflationary pressures until "late this year and in 1998."

That prompted renewed debate among economists and reversed the views of a few experts who had been calling for no move in March. Overall, however, the Fed chief's latest comments did not change many minds.
Current inflation indicators remain tame, and pipeline pressures are hard to detect, said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at NationsBanc Capital Markets Inc.
"I would definitely call it preemptive," he said. "I don't think there was any evidence (Wednesday) morning that inflation is increasing."

Kretzmer was referring to Wednesday's report on consumer prices for February, which showed the overall Consumer Price Index climbed 0.3 percent and the core index rose 0.2 percent. Wall Street economists had been expecting a 0.2 percent increase in both measures.

In light of the benign data, central bankers might vote to raise rates believing that "a move right now would maintain credibility and maybe even lower inflation further in the future," Kretzmer said.
He projected a 25-basis-points fed funds rate hike on March 25, but called for an ease sometime in the fall.
While the economists agreed that a rate hike now would be preemptive, most also agreed that fears of an uptick in inflation are well-supported by economic data aside from the inflation reports.
Many analysts fingered the typical scapegoats -- signs of wage pressures and swift economic growth -- as good reasons to expect a policy shift.
"The growth numbers ... and the average hourly earnings have been trending up," said Henry Willmore, senior economist at BZW Securities Inc.
Willmore added that the Fed's most recent Beige Book report on economic activity in the various federal regions, released last week, revealed pockets of labor-market tightness.
"Although the summary was kind of bland, it seems in fact ... that most districts are experiencing some upward wage pressures," he said.
In particular, recent data on retail sales and jobless claims, as well as speeches by Fed officials, have pushed many experts to change their views on the March meeting.
"All of the sudden you've got too many people using the 'preemptive' word," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
Still, most analysts in the survey concurred that the economy is not a runaway train and central bankers can be relied upon to use a light touch on the brakes.

"I don't think it's a question of having to take away the punch bowl; I think it's more like having to take some of the vodka out of it," said Tim O'Neill, chief economist at the Bank of Montreal/Harris Bank in Toronto.
O'Neill, who had been predicting the Fed would hold rates steady for the rest of 1997, revised his forecast and is now expecting a 5.75-percent federal funds rate before year's end.

"We're expecting a 50-basis-point hike in two pieces of 25," O'Neill said, adding that the risk is that the U.S. central bank will have to raise rates by as much as 75 basis points before the end of 1997.
Still, O'Neill said he favored "two 25s and then a wait-and-see" posture.
The survey was conducted between Wednesday morning and early Thursday afternoon. Firms that forecast no move were called after the Greenspan testimony to verify their projections, except where noted.
